$comment: Complaint log. process.unpunished is DERIVED - see METHODOLOGY.md section 8 - and is recomputed and checked by scripts/validate.mjs.

complaints.title: Closure of the federal forum to persons of African descent

jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States

count.collective_note: Formally, every person of African descent then living in the United States, free or enslaved.

harmed.collective: Persons of African descent within the United States
harmed.interstitial: Every injury suffered by a person of African descent between 1857 and 1868 that went unheard because this holding closed the forum. Those injuries have no entries anywhere, and cannot be counted.

respondents.described: Chief Justice Roger B. Taney and the concurring majority, acting in judicial capacity

named.name: Roger B. Taney
named.role: Chief Justice of the United States; author of the opinion
named.note: Named as author of the holding. The conduct was lawful judicial action; no offence is charged in this entry.

process.forum: Supreme Court of the United States
process.narrative: No process was possible, because the holding was itself the act complained of. It is entered first in this book because it establishes the condition every earlier complaint was decided under and every later one had to overcome: not that the injury was excused, but that no forum would hear it.

granted: Superseded by the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Amendments and the Civil Rights Act of 1866
remedy.outstanding: The decision was never overruled by the Court; it was displaced by constitutional amendment.

complaints.status_note: Citation: Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857).
complaints.offense_note: Not a violent act. The entry records a lawful judicial holding that operated as the precondition for the violence in every entry below. It is carried here because a log that recorded only the blows and not the rule that made them unanswerable would be incomplete.
complaints.conduct: The Court held that persons of African descent, whether enslaved or free, were not and could not become citizens within the meaning of Article III, and therefore could not invoke the jurisdiction of the federal courts; and further that Congress lacked power to prohibit slavery in the territories.

restoration.reached: No individual. The holding was displaced by constitutional amendment, which restored nothing to the Scotts.

concurrence.agree: The holding is the judicial record itself; there is no divergence as to what was decided.
concurrence.diverge: Sources diverge on Taney's motive and on whether the territorial holding was necessary to the judgment. The book does not resolve it.

complaints.title: Chattel enslavement in the United States and its colonial predecessors

place.note: The slaveholding colonies and states, and the domestic trade between them

count.note: Approximately 3.9 million persons were enslaved in the United States at the 1860 census. The number of persons enslaved across the full period is larger by an order that this book does not estimate.

harmed.collective: Enslaved persons in North America and their descendants
harmed.interstitial: Wealth transferred and still held. Names not preserved and now unrecoverable. Kinship lines severed by sale, which is why descendants of this entry frequently cannot document the ancestry that a claim would require of them.

transmitted.description: Kinship lines severed by sale, so descent cannot be documented by people from whom documentation is now demanded. Wealth transferred and compounding for a further eight generations. And the claim this book cannot itself establish: that trauma sustained across generations without opportunity to heal produces adaptive behaviours that outlive the conditions that required them - DeGruy's vacant esteem, ever-present anger, and racist socialisation.
transmitted.note: Standing is argued_in_literature, not documented. Post Traumatic Slave Syndrome is an influential and widely taught framework and is not a diagnostic category; parts of the transmission literature it draws on are actively contested. The book records the argument and its status, and does not convert it into a finding.

respondents.described: Slaveholders; slave traders; sheriffs, patrols, and courts enforcing the slave codes; legislatures enacting them; insurers, banks, and shippers financing the trade

process.narrative: There was no forum. The conduct was lawful where it occurred and its victims lacked the legal capacity to complain of it. This entry exists because a log of unpunished crimes that omitted it on the ground that it was not then a crime would be reproducing the impediment rather than recording it.

sought: General Orders No. 15 (Special Field Orders No. 15), 1865, rescinded the same year
H.R. 40, introduced in every Congress since 1989, never enacted
granted: Abolition by the Thirteenth Amendment, which is not compensation
remedy.outstanding: No compensation was ever paid to any enslaved person by the United States. Compensation was paid to slaveholders in the District of Columbia under the Compensated Emancipation Act of 1862.

complaints.status_note: The register cannot be completed for this entry and never will be. Named individuals appear where a narrative, register, petition, or bill of sale preserved a name; the overwhelming majority did not. See PR-COLLECTIVE-ENSLAVED-US.
complaints.conduct: Holding of persons as property; compelled uncompensated labor; sale and separation of families; sexual violence without cognizable offense; killing and maiming under statutes that graded such acts as damage to property or excused them entirely; and denial of the legal capacity to testify, contract, marry, or sue.

restoration.reached: Nobody. No compensation was ever paid to any enslaved person by the United States; compensation was paid to slaveholders in the District of Columbia in 1862.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

concurrence.agree: Victim testimony, administrative record and the perpetrating institutions' own ledgers agree on the constituent conduct.
concurrence.diverge: The narrative corpus and the administrative corpus diverge systematically in what they record: the ledgers preserve numbers and prices, the narratives preserve names, kinship and violence. Neither is complete, and the ledger's completeness is a feature of who kept it.

complaints.title: Kidnapping of Solomon Northup and the failure of the prosecution

place.note: Kidnapped in Washington; held in Rapides and Avoyelles Parishes, Louisiana

harmed.collective: Free Black citizens of the northern states, of whom an unknown number were kidnapped and sold and never recovered
harmed.interstitial: Twelve years of a life. An unknown number of other free Black northerners kidnapped in the same trade who were never recovered and so left no narrative, no prosecution, and no entry.

respondents.described: James H. Birch, the trader who sold him in Washington; Alexander Merrill and Joseph Russell, charged in New York with the kidnapping

named.name: James H. Birch
named.note: Acquitted because Northup, the only witness, was barred by District law from testifying against him.

named.name: Alexander Merrill
named.note: Prosecuted in New York from 1854; the case ended without conviction after years of jurisdictional contest.

process.forum: Criminal court, District of Columbia (1853); Saratoga and Washington County courts, New York (1854-1857)
process.narrative: Birch was charged in Washington and acquitted. The reason is the whole of this entry: Northup, the only witness to his own kidnapping, was barred by District law from testifying against a white man. Birch was permitted to testify in his own defence. The subsequent New York prosecution of Merrill and Russell was obstructed for years by contests over jurisdiction between the two states and ended without a conviction.

sought: Criminal prosecution in the District of Columbia, 1853
granted: Recovery of his liberty, by executive action of the Governor of New York under an 1840 statute
remedy.outstanding: No conviction. No compensation for twelve years of uncompensated labour. Northup's own date and place of death are unknown.

complaints.status_note: Entered as the cleanest single illustration of the difference this book records. The crime was documented, the perpetrator was named, the forum was open, and the victim was silenced by a rule of evidence. Twelve Years a Slave (1853) is the complaint he filed instead, and it is the one that survived.
complaints.conduct: Solomon Northup, a free citizen of New York, was drugged, seized, held in a slave pen within sight of the Capitol, and sold south. He was held in slavery for twelve years until his identity was established and he was recovered by an agent of the Governor of New York.

restoration.reached: Solomon Northup alone, by executive action of the Governor of New York. No other kidnapped free northerner in the record was recovered.

concurrence.agree: Northup's narrative, the New York executive record and the District prosecution agree on the kidnapping and the twelve years.
concurrence.diverge: Birch's account, given in his own defence, contradicts Northup's throughout. It prevailed because Northup was barred from answering it, so the divergence was never tested on the evidence.

complaints.title: Colfax massacre and the reversal of the convictions

jurisdiction: United States (Circuit Court, District of Louisiana)

count.note: Counts vary by source. Most of the dead were killed after surrender.

harmed.interstitial: The collapse of Reconstruction enforcement in Louisiana. Cruikshank's holding then travelled outward from these dead and disposed of prosecutions in states that had nothing to do with Grant Parish.

respondents.described: Members of the attacking force, including former Confederate soldiers and members of the White League

process.forum: United States Circuit Court, District of Louisiana; Supreme Court of the United States
process.narrative: Federal prosecutions under the Enforcement Act of 1870 produced three convictions. In United States v. Cruikshank, 92 U.S. 542 (1876), the Supreme Court set them aside, holding that the Fourteenth Amendment reached only state action and that the indictment failed to charge a federal offense. No one was ever punished for the killings.

remedy.outstanding: None sought or obtained. A Louisiana state marker erected in 1950 described the event as a riot and was removed in 2021.

complaints.status_note: The controlling entry for the state action impediment: the case that created the doctrine is the case in which the only convictions were lost.
complaints.conduct: An armed white force attacked Black state militia and freedmen defending the Grant Parish courthouse following the disputed 1872 Louisiana election, and killed a large number of them, most after they had surrendered.

restoration.reached: Nobody. The 1950 state marker calling the killings a riot was removed in 2021, so even the symbolic record was withdrawn rather than corrected.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

concurrence.agree: Federal indictments, congressional inquiry and press across the political spectrum agree that a mass killing occurred and that most died after surrender.
concurrence.diverge: The count diverges from roughly 60 to 150. No source is independent of the fact that no official count was attempted.

complaints.title: Killing of Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell, and William Stewart

harmed.collective: The Black business community of the Curve, Memphis
harmed.interstitial: The People's Grocery was sold at a fraction of its value to the competitor whose hostility produced the killings. Several thousand Black residents left Memphis. Neither the transfer nor the exodus appears in any register of loss.

respondents.described: Members of the mob; the sheriff and jailers who surrendered custody of prisoners in their charge

process.narrative: No one was charged. Prisoners in lawful state custody were handed over to a mob by the officers responsible for them, which is the paradigm case of an official acting beyond the authority of the office.

remedy.outstanding: None. The killings caused a mass departure of Black residents from Memphis and began Ida B. Wells's investigative work.

complaints.status_note: Wells was godmother to Thomas Moss's daughter. Her investigation of these killings produced the analytical method this record book uses.
complaints.conduct: Three Black grocers, held in the Shelby County jail after a confrontation arising from white competitors' hostility to their store, were taken from the jail by a mob and killed. The competing grocer's business interest in eliminating the People's Grocery is documented as the motive.

restoration.reached: Nobody. The store was sold at a fraction of its value to the competitor whose hostility produced the killings.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

concurrence.agree: Wells's investigation and the Memphis daily press agree on the abduction from the jail and the killings.
concurrence.diverge: They diverge entirely on cause: the press offered a criminal pretext, Wells established commercial rivalry. This is the entry where the hostile vantage's own reporting was turned against the finding it was written to support.

complaints.title: Destruction of the Memphis Free Speech and banishment of its editor

harmed.interstitial: The issues the Free Speech would have printed. Every killing in west Tennessee that went uninvestigated in the decades after its only investigator was driven out.

respondents.described: Members of the mob, organized following publication of a call to action in a Memphis daily newspaper

process.narrative: No charges. No compensation for the destroyed property. The exile was effective and permanent.

remedy.outstanding: None. Wells was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize special citation in 2020.

complaints.status_note: Entered because the suppression of the record is itself an injury this book is in the business of recording.
complaints.conduct: After the Free Speech published an editorial disputing the rape pretext offered for lynchings, a mob destroyed the newspaper's press and office and threatened the life of its editor, who was then travelling. She was warned not to return to Memphis and did not return for decades.

restoration.reached: Ida B. Wells posthumously, by Pulitzer special citation in 2020. The press was never replaced and the exile was never lifted in her lifetime.

concurrence.agree: Wells's account and the surviving Memphis press agree that the office was destroyed and that a call to action preceded it.
concurrence.diverge: No independent non-hostile vantage survives, because the vantage that would have produced it is the thing destroyed.

complaints.title: Wilmington massacre and overthrow of the municipal government

count.note: The 2006 state commission was unable to fix a figure; contemporary and later estimates diverge widely.

harmed.collective: Black residents of Wilmington and the elected officials removed
harmed.interstitial: Property abandoned under threat and never recovered. A Black professional and political class that did not re-form in Wilmington. The statewide disenfranchisement campaign this was staged to deliver, which succeeded.

transmitted.description: A Black professional and political class that did not re-form in Wilmington. The statewide disenfranchisement the coup was staged to deliver, which succeeded and structured North Carolina politics for six decades.

respondents.described: Leaders of the Democratic Party campaign, the Wilmington Light Infantry, and Red Shirts; several participants held or subsequently took public office

named.name: Alfred Moore Waddell
named.role: Leader of the armed force; installed as mayor the same day
named.note: Named by the state commission as a leader of the coup. Never charged; held the mayoralty afterward.

process.narrative: No one was charged. The leaders held office afterward. It is the only successful overthrow of a municipal government in United States history, and it produced no prosecution.

granted: State commission report, 2006, acknowledging the events
remedy.outstanding: No compensation. The commission's recommendations for economic redress were not enacted.

complaints.conduct: An armed white force killed Black residents, destroyed the offices of the Daily Record, forced the elected biracial municipal government to resign at gunpoint, installed replacements, and banished named Black and white residents from the city.

restoration.reached: Nobody materially. The 2006 commission acknowledged the events; its recommendations for economic redress were not enacted.

concurrence.agree: The 2006 state commission, contemporaneous press and the perpetrators' own published accounts agree on the coup, the killings and the banishments.
concurrence.diverge: The death toll diverges from roughly 60 to 300. The perpetrators' accounts are unusually forthcoming because they were written as boasts, which makes them strong on conduct and unreliable on count.

complaints.title: Killing of Mary Turner and the Brooks-Lowndes lynchings

count.note: At least eleven people were killed over the week; sources differ on the total.

harmed.collective: Black residents of Brooks and Lowndes Counties, several hundred of whom left the area
harmed.interstitial: Several hundred Black residents left Brooks and Lowndes Counties in the following weeks, abandoning crops mid-season. Mary Turner's stated intention to swear out warrants is the last recorded attempt by anyone to use a court in that county for these killings.

respondents.described: Members of the mob. Walter White's investigation for the NAACP obtained the names of participants and transmitted them to the Governor of Georgia.

named.name: [Names withheld in source]
named.note: Walter White's field investigation obtained participants' names and transmitted them to the Governor of Georgia. The NAACP did not publish them and no prosecution followed. The record therefore holds an accusation whose subjects were identified to the state and never charged.

process.narrative: No one was charged, notwithstanding that the NAACP delivered a list of named participants to the state. The Department of Justice declined to act. This entry is the clearest demonstration that the impediment was not the difficulty of identification.

granted: Georgia historical marker, 2010, later repeatedly vandalized and removed in 2020

complaints.status_note: Mary Turner was killed for announcing an intention to use the courts. The record book notes this without comment.
complaints.conduct: During a week of lynchings following the killing of a plantation owner, Mary Turner publicly denounced the killing of her husband Hayes Turner and said she would seek warrants against those responsible. A mob seized her the next day and killed her. She was in the eighth month of pregnancy; her unborn child was killed as well.

restoration.reached: Nobody. A 2010 historical marker was repeatedly vandalised and was removed in 2020.

concurrence.agree: The NAACP field investigation and contemporaneous press agree on the sequence and on the manner of the killing.
concurrence.diverge: The press reported the killings as responses to a crime; the investigation established that Mary Turner was killed for announcing she would swear out warrants. The divergence is the pretext.

complaints.title: Elaine massacre and the capital convictions of the survivors

count.note: No official count was made. Five white men also died.

harmed.collective: Black sharecroppers and residents of Phillips County
harmed.interstitial: The union that the meeting was called to form. No coroner's inquest was held for any of the dead and no burial was recorded, so the absence of a count is not a gap in this book's research but a fact about what was done.

respondents.described: Members of posses drawn from Phillips and surrounding counties; United States Army troops; county officers conducting the interrogations

process.forum: Phillips County Circuit Court; Supreme Court of the United States
process.narrative: No participant in the killings was charged. Instead, 122 Black residents were indicted and twelve were sentenced to death after trials lasting minutes before all-white juries surrounded by a mob. In Moore v. Dempsey, 261 U.S. 86 (1923), the Supreme Court held that a trial dominated by mob pressure denies due process, and the convictions were eventually undone. The outcome recorded here is the vacatur of the victims' convictions; no perpetrator was ever tried.

granted: Release of the twelve condemned men by 1925
Moore v. Dempsey established federal habeas review of mob-dominated trials
remedy.outstanding: No compensation to any victim or descendant. No count of the dead was ever made.

complaints.status_note: Records the inversion this book exists to document: the survivors were the only people prosecuted.
complaints.conduct: Black sharecroppers meeting to organize the Progressive Farmers and Household Union of America were attacked; posses and federal troops killed a large number of Black residents across the county over several days. Survivors were arrested, and confessions were obtained by torture.

restoration.reached: The twelve condemned men, released by 1925. Nothing reached the families of the dead, who were never counted.

concurrence.agree: Moore v. Dempsey, the NAACP investigation and press agree that the trials were mob-dominated and the confessions tortured.
concurrence.diverge: The count of the dead diverges from roughly 100 to 240, and the framing diverges absolutely: contemporaneous white press reported an insurrection, the investigation established a massacre of people meeting to form a union.

complaints.title: Ocoee election day massacre

count.note: Estimates diverge sharply; no official count was made.

harmed.collective: The Black community of Ocoee, permanently displaced
harmed.interstitial: Title to the land of the displaced passed to white owners and was never recovered. Ocoee's Black population fell to effectively zero and stayed there for decades, which means the harm continued to be inflicted on people who were never present at the event.

transmitted.description: Title to the expropriated land passed to white owners and was never disturbed. Ocoee's Black population stood at effectively zero for decades, so the exclusion continued to be enforced against people born long after the killings.

respondents.described: Members of the mob, including Ku Klux Klan participants; a deputy sheriff took Perry from custody

process.narrative: No charges. Ocoee remained effectively closed to Black residents for decades.

granted: Florida legislation in 2020 requiring instruction on the massacre in public schools
remedy.outstanding: No compensation for the land and homes lost. Title to much of the expropriated property passed to white owners and was never recovered.

complaints.conduct: After Black residents attempted to vote, a white mob attacked the Black district of Ocoee, burned homes, a church, and a lodge, killed residents, and lynched July Perry. The surviving Black population was driven out and did not return.

restoration.reached: Nobody materially. Florida legislated in 2020 that the massacre be taught in schools. Title to the expropriated land was never disturbed.

concurrence.agree: Contemporary press and later scholarship agree on the lynching of July Perry, the burning of the district and the permanent expulsion.
concurrence.diverge: The count diverges by an order of magnitude, from 6 to 60. The census corroborates the expulsion independently of any account of the violence.

complaints.title: Destruction of the Greenwood District, Tulsa

count.note: The 2001 Commission recorded 39 confirmed deaths and reviewed estimates ranging to 300. More than 1,250 homes were destroyed and roughly 6,000 people were detained.

harmed.collective: Residents and property owners of the Greenwood District
harmed.interstitial: Insurance denied under riot clauses, converting destruction into total uncompensated loss. Deeds and records burned with the district, so the proof of ownership that a later claim would require was destroyed by the same act that created the claim.

transmitted.description: Greenwood's accumulated commercial wealth was destroyed in a night and never rebuilt to its prior extent. Deeds burned with the district, so descendants cannot produce the proof of ownership a claim requires - the same act created the claim and destroyed its evidence.

respondents.described: Members of the mob; city officials who deputized them and issued arms; National Guard units

process.forum: Tulsa County; Oklahoma; United States District Court, Northern District of Oklahoma
process.narrative: No one was convicted of any killing or of the destruction. A grand jury convened in 1921 attributed the cause to Black residents. Federal litigation by survivors was dismissed as time-barred and certiorari was denied in Alexander v. Oklahoma, 382 F.3d 1206 (10th Cir. 2004). A later state public nuisance action brought by survivors was dismissed by the Oklahoma Supreme Court in 2024.

sought: Compensation recommended by the Oklahoma Commission, 2001
granted: State commission report and scholarships; no direct compensation to survivors or descendants
remedy.outstanding: Property losses were never compensated by insurers or by the state. Survivors of the massacre were still living when the 2024 dismissal was entered.

complaints.status_note: The entry in which every impediment in this book operates at once: no prosecution, no insurance, no standing, no timeliness, no immunity waiver.
complaints.conduct: A white mob, including men deputized by city officials and armed from public and private stocks, destroyed the thirty-five block Greenwood District, killed residents, and detained thousands of survivors in internment camps. Aircraft were used over the district.

restoration.reached: Nobody materially. Commission report and scholarships; no payment to any survivor or descendant. Survivors were still living when the Oklahoma Supreme Court dismissed their action in 2024.

concurrence.agree: The 2001 state commission, insurance records, contemporaneous press and survivor testimony agree on the destruction, the detentions and the denial of claims.
concurrence.diverge: The death toll diverges from 39 confirmed to 300 estimated. The mass grave investigations are the only vantage still capable of resolving it, and they are physical rather than documentary.

complaints.title: Destruction of Rosewood, Florida

count.note: Six Black and two white deaths were confirmed by the 1993 study; survivor accounts describe a considerably higher toll.

harmed.collective: The residents and landowners of Rosewood
harmed.interstitial: A town that ceased to exist. Survivors dispersed under conditions that made them unlocatable for seventy years, which is why the 1994 compensation reached so few of them.

transmitted.description: Survivors dispersed under conditions that made them unlocatable for seventy years, which is why the 1994 compensation reached so few. Several families concealed their Rosewood origins for generations.

respondents.described: Members of the mob drawn from surrounding counties; the Levy County sheriff, who declined to intervene

process.narrative: A 1923 grand jury returned no indictments. No one was ever prosecuted. Seventy-one years later the Florida Legislature enacted the Rosewood Compensation Act of 1994, providing payments to survivors, a property-loss claims process, and a scholarship fund for descendants.

sought: Claim bill before the Florida Legislature, 1993-1994
granted: Rosewood Compensation Act of 1994: payments to survivors, a property claims process, and the Rosewood Family Scholarship Fund
remedy.outstanding: No criminal accountability. Compensation was partial and reached a small number of claimants.

complaints.status_note: The precedent entry. Rosewood is the clearest American instance of legislative reparation for a specific massacre, and it demonstrates the route that Tulsa litigation could not take. Note the outcome value: legislative_remedy is still unpunished, because no perpetrator was tried.
complaints.conduct: Following an allegation by a white woman in nearby Sumner, a white mob attacked the Black town of Rosewood over several days, killed residents, and burned the town. Survivors fled into the swamps and the town ceased to exist.

restoration.reached: A small number of located survivors and descendants, under the 1994 Act. Most claims were unmet and most of the dispersed were never found.

concurrence.agree: The 1993 legislative study and survivor testimony given in 1993 and 1994 agree on the attack, the burning and the flight.
concurrence.diverge: Confirmed deaths number 8; survivor accounts describe substantially more. The legislature adopted the lower figure and compensated on that basis.

complaints.title: United States Public Health Service Untreated Syphilis Study at Tuskegee

count.note: 399 men with syphilis and 201 controls. Wives and children were infected in consequence; the exact number was never established.

harmed.collective: The enrolled men, their wives, and children born with congenital syphilis
harmed.interstitial: Wives infected and children born with congenital syphilis, never fully enumerated. A documented and persisting withdrawal of trust in public medicine among Black Americans, which is a harm to people who were never enrolled.

transmitted.description: Wives infected and children born with congenital syphilis, never enumerated. A measured and persisting withdrawal of trust in public medicine among Black Americans, documented in health-services research - a harm falling on people who were never enrolled and were not born when the study ended.

respondents.described: Officers and physicians of the United States Public Health Service, acting in official capacity over forty years

process.forum: United States District Court, Middle District of Alabama; congressional oversight
process.narrative: No one was criminally prosecuted. The study ended in 1972 after press disclosure. A class action settled in 1974 for approximately $10 million with lifetime medical benefits for participants and affected family members. A presidential apology followed in 1997.

granted: 1974 settlement, approximately $10 million
Tuskegee Health Benefit Program
Presidential apology, 16 May 1997
remedy.outstanding: No criminal accountability for any officer. The study prompted the National Research Act of 1974 and the Belmont Report.

complaints.status_note: Cites the perpetrating agency's own study records, held by NARA Southeast and the CDC. Entered as the clearest instance of officials acting beyond the statute of their role over a forty-year span with no criminal consequence.
complaints.conduct: The Public Health Service enrolled approximately 600 Black men, 399 with latent syphilis, under the representation that they were being treated for bad blood. They were not treated. When penicillin became the standard of care in the 1940s, the Service acted to keep participants from receiving it, including through arrangements with local physicians and draft boards, in order to observe the untreated course of the disease to autopsy.

restoration.reached: Enrolled participants and some affected family, under the 1974 settlement and the Tuskegee Health Benefit Program. Wives infected and children born with congenital syphilis were never fully enumerated and so could not be reached.

concurrence.agree: The perpetrating agency's own forty-year records, the 1972 press disclosure and the congressional inquiry agree in full on the design and the withholding of treatment.
concurrence.diverge: There is effectively no divergence. This is the rare entry whose strongest vantage is the perpetrator's own meticulous record, kept because the men were regarded as subjects rather than as parties who might one day read it.

complaints.title: Moore's Ford Bridge killings

harmed.collective: Black farm workers of Walton County
harmed.interstitial: The 1946 grand jury records remain sealed. Participants were reportedly known within the county and are now dead, so the identification that 2,790 interviews did not produce can no longer be produced at all.

respondents.described: Members of the mob, estimated in the dozens; participants were reportedly known within the county

process.forum: Walton County; United States (FBI investigation, 1946; DOJ review under the Till Act, 2000s)
process.narrative: President Truman ordered an FBI investigation. Agents interviewed some 2,790 people over four months. The federal grand jury returned no indictments. The case was reopened under the Emmett Till Unsolved Civil Rights Crime Act and closed again without charges. It remains the last mass lynching in the United States and it is unsolved.

granted: Federal investigation; no charges
remedy.outstanding: Everything. Litigation over release of the sealed 1946 grand jury records was rejected by the Eleventh Circuit en banc in 2020.

complaints.status_note: The killings contributed directly to Truman's Executive Order 9808 establishing the President's Committee on Civil Rights.
complaints.conduct: A mob stopped a car carrying two Black couples and shot all four at close range. Dorothy Malcom was pregnant.

restoration.reached: Nobody. The 1946 grand jury records remain sealed; the Eleventh Circuit rejected the action to unseal them in 2020.
restoration.none_note: No form of restoration was ever made.

concurrence.agree: The FBI investigation, press and later scholarship agree on the killings and on the scale of the mob.
concurrence.diverge: No vantage names a participant. 2,790 interviews produced no indictment, and the grand jury record that might explain why remains sealed.

complaints.title: Groveland Four

jurisdiction: Supreme Court of the United States

harmed.interstitial: Sheriff McCall remained in office for twenty-one years after the shooting and the deaths in his custody during that period are separately documented. Charles Greenlee lived to be refused clemency repeatedly and died seven years before the pardons issued.

respondents.described: Sheriff Willis V. McCall and deputies of Lake County, acting under color of law

named.name: Willis V. McCall
named.note: Shot Samuel Shepherd and Walter Irvin while they were handcuffed in his custody. Cleared by a coroner's inquest, never charged, remained sheriff until 1972. Irvin survived and contradicted his account.

process.forum: Lake County Circuit Court; Supreme Court of the United States; Florida Clemency Board; Lake County Circuit Court (2021)
process.narrative: A coroner's inquest cleared McCall of the shooting; he was never prosecuted and remained sheriff until 1972. Irvin was retried, convicted again, and later paroled. Florida issued posthumous pardons in 2019, and in 2021 a court formally exonerated all four and dismissed the indictments. No officer was ever charged for the shooting or for the beatings.

granted: Posthumous pardons, 2019
Judicial exoneration and dismissal of indictments, 2021
Florida claim bill compensating the families, 2023
remedy.outstanding: No criminal accountability for any officer. Exoneration corrected the state's injury to the victims and left the perpetrators' conduct unaddressed.

complaints.status_note: Outcome is recorded as posthumous_exoneration and therefore still counts as unpunished. See METHODOLOGY.md section 8 for why.
complaints.conduct: Four young Black men were accused of rape on evidence later found to be without foundation. Ernest Thomas was pursued and killed by a posse. The three others were beaten in custody to obtain confessions. After the Supreme Court reversed the convictions in Shepherd v. Florida, 341 U.S. 50 (1951), Sheriff Willis McCall shot Samuel Shepherd and Walter Irvin while transporting them in handcuffs; Shepherd died and Irvin survived and contradicted the sheriff's account.

restoration.reached: The four men posthumously, by pardon in 2019 and exoneration in 2021; their families by Florida claim bill in 2023. Charles Greenlee was refused clemency repeatedly and died seven years before the pardons.

concurrence.agree: The litigation record, Supreme Court reversal, FBI file and later exoneration proceedings agree on the beatings and on the shooting in custody.
concurrence.diverge: The sheriff's account of the shooting and Walter Irvin's directly contradict one another. Irvin survived to testify; the coroner's inquest credited the sheriff.

complaints.title: Killing of Emmett Till

harmed.interstitial: Bryant and Milam were paid for the confession. Mamie Till-Mobley spent the remaining forty-eight years of her life producing the record that the acquittal had refused to produce.

respondents.described: Roy Bryant and J.W. Milam, tried and acquitted; other participants named in later scholarship were never charged

named.name: Roy Bryant
named.note: Acquitted in 1955, then described committing the killing in a paid magazine interview in 1956. Double jeopardy barred retrial.

process.forum: Circuit Court of Tallahatchie County; federal grand jury, 2006-2007; DOJ review closed 2021
process.narrative: An all-white, all-male jury acquitted Bryant and Milam after deliberating slightly over an hour. Months later, protected by double jeopardy, both described committing the killing in a paid interview published in Look magazine. The Department of Justice reopened the matter twice and closed it in December 2021 without charges.

granted: Emmett Till Unsolved Civil Rights Crime Act of 2007
Emmett Till Antilynching Act, Pub. L. 117-107 (2022), making lynching a federal hate crime
Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument, 2023
remedy.outstanding: No one was ever punished. Mamie Till-Mobley's decision to hold an open-casket funeral, and to permit the photographs to be published, is the reason the record exists at all.

complaints.status_note: The confession is documented and the acquittal is final. This is the entry that demonstrates that in this book unpunished never means unproven.
complaints.conduct: A fourteen-year-old boy visiting from Chicago was taken from his great-uncle's house at night, beaten, shot, and sunk in the Tallahatchie River, following an allegation about an encounter at a store in Money.

restoration.reached: No individual. The Till Act (2007), the Emmett Till Antilynching Act (2022) and a national monument (2023) reached the law and the landscape, not the family.

concurrence.agree: The trial record, the perpetrators' paid confession and the DOJ reviews agree that Bryant and Milam abducted and killed Emmett Till.
concurrence.diverge: The confession and the acquittal are in flat contradiction, and both stand: the acquittal is final in law and the confession is final in fact. Later scholarship diverges on how many others participated; none was ever charged.

complaints.title: Framing and imprisonment of Clyde Kennard

harmed.interstitial: The degree awarded to nobody. The Sovereignty Commission operated for a further seventeen years on legislative appropriation, and its files record other arrangements of the same kind.

respondents.described: Officials of the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission, a state agency, and cooperating local law enforcement and prosecutors

named.name: Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission
named.role: Agency of the State of Mississippi
named.note: The Commission's own files, opened by court order in 1998, document its arrangement of the prosecution. A lawfully constituted state agency funded by the legislature; no officer was charged.

process.forum: Forrest County Circuit Court; Forrest County Circuit Court (2006)
process.narrative: The conviction was vacated in 2006 after the sole witness recanted and the Sovereignty Commission's own files, opened by court order in 1998, documented the arrangement. Kennard died in 1963. No official was ever prosecuted for procuring the conviction.

granted: Vacatur of conviction, 2006
remedy.outstanding: No accountability for any official. The agency that arranged it was a lawfully constituted arm of the State of Mississippi, funded by the legislature.

complaints.status_note: The Sovereignty Commission files are the rare case where the impediment documented itself. Held by the Mississippi Department of Archives and History.
complaints.conduct: After Clyde Kennard applied repeatedly to enroll at Mississippi Southern College, state officials, acting through the Mississippi State Sovereignty Commission, arranged his prosecution for accessory to the theft of chicken feed valued at twenty-five dollars. He was sentenced to seven years at hard labor. He developed colon cancer in prison and was denied adequate care.

restoration.reached: Clyde Kennard posthumously, by vacatur in 2006, forty-three years after he died at thirty-six. The degree he applied for was awarded to nobody.

concurrence.agree: The Sovereignty Commission's own files, the recanting witness and the 2006 vacatur agree that the prosecution was arranged.
concurrence.diverge: The trial record and the agency record contradict each other completely. The agency record prevailed only because a court ordered the files opened thirty-five years later.

complaints.title: Aggregate record: 3,224 lynchings, 1889-1918

place.note: Recorded across the United States, concentrated in the former Confederate states

count.note: 702 of those recorded were white. The compilation is acknowledged by its own authors to undercount, as it depends on press reporting.

harmed.collective: Persons lynched in the United States, 1889-1918
harmed.interstitial: The departures, the crops left, the businesses sold under duress, and the testimony never given, none of which any of the three competing tallies attempted to count.

respondents.described: Mobs, in the great majority of cases never identified in any official record; officers who surrendered custody in a substantial number of cases

process.narrative: Prosecutions were exceptional and convictions nearly unknown. Federal anti-lynching legislation was introduced repeatedly from 1918 and was defeated by filibuster on every occasion until 2022.

sought: Dyer Anti-Lynching Bill, passed the House in 1922, filibustered in the Senate
granted: Senate resolution of apology, 2005
Emmett Till Antilynching Act, 2022
remedy.outstanding: The apology came eighty-seven years after the compilation was published. This entry stands for every killing in it that has no entry of its own.

complaints.status_note: An aggregate entry, entered under the rule in METHODOLOGY.md section 9: where sources preserve only a count, the count is recorded as a count and is not permitted to stand in for individuated persons.
complaints.conduct: Killing of persons by mobs outside any legal process, as enumerated by the NAACP's compilation of press and investigative records over thirty years.

restoration.reached: No individual among the 3,224. A Senate resolution of apology in 2005 and a federal offence in 2022, eighty-seven and one hundred and four years after the compilation was published.

concurrence.agree: The NAACP, Tuskegee Institute and EJI series agree on the pattern and on the near-total absence of prosecution.
concurrence.diverge: The three tallies diverge in count because they diverge in definition and coverage. All three depend on press reporting and all three state that they undercount; the divergence measures the reporting, not the killing.
